lessons.title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a closed skill?
A) A football player receiving a through pass from a teammate
B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat
C) A hockey player hitting a moving ball past a goalkeeper
D) A basketball player taking a free throw during a fast break
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ability' in the context of sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: ability is an innate / natural / inherited characteristic. 1 mark for development: it is stable and largely unchangeable; it underpins a performer's potential to learn and perform skills (accept: it sets a ceiling on what a performer can achieve). Do not credit definitions that describe ability as learned or practised.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use the four skill classification continuums to analyse a performer's front crawl stroke.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each continuum correctly applied with a brief justification (max 3 continuums credited). Examples: Basic/complex — complex, because it requires simultaneous coordination of arm pull, leg kick, breathing pattern and head position (1). Open/closed — closed, because the pool environment is stable and the performer moves through predictable conditions (1). Self-paced/externally paced — self-paced, because the swimmer decides their own stroke rate and turn timing (1). Gross/fine — gross, because large muscle groups of the arms, shoulders, core and legs produce the movement (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a basketball player taking a free throw is classified differently on the open/closed continuum compared to the same player making a lay-up during open play. Use the definitions of open and closed skills in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a free throw is a closed skill. 1 mark for justification: the environment is stable and predictable; the player stands at the same spot, no defenders can challenge, and the timing is self-controlled. 1 mark for identifying that a lay-up in open play is an open skill (or further towards the open end). 1 mark for justification: the environment is unpredictable; defenders are moving, teammates are repositioning, and the player must adapt their movement and timing to the changing situation.

practice_questions.text: A Year-10 PE teacher is designing classification tasks for two groups: one group will practise hitting a stationary ball on a tee, the other will practise hitting a ball bowled at them by a partner. Analyse how the four continuums differ between these two tasks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses all four continuums, clearly differentiating both tasks on each, with precise definitions and specific justifications rooted in the scenario. Points might include: basic/complex — hitting a stationary ball is more basic (fewer decisions, simpler movement), while hitting a bowled ball is more complex (timing judgement, footwork, range of shots possible); open/closed — stationary ball is closed (environment controlled, ball position fixed), bowled ball is open (ball direction, speed, bounce variable); self-paced/externally paced — tee hit is self-paced (performer starts when ready), bowled ball is externally paced (bowler dictates timing); gross/fine — both are gross skills (large muscle groups driving the shot) but the tee hit may be slightly more fine near the point of contact. Consistent reference to both tasks throughout.

Secure: Correctly analyses at least three continuums, with most justifications accurate. Generally applies to both tasks but may be less precise on one or two.

Developing: Names and partially explains two or three continuums. May label without justifying, or analyse only one task.

Emerging: Names one or two continuums; limited or no justification; may confuse continuum definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old club athlete competes in both archery and rugby union. Evaluate the view that classifying skills on the four continuums helps coaches plan training more effectively than simply labelling skills as 'easy' or 'hard'. Use examples from both sports in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to specific sporting examples from archery and/or rugby, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the four continuums reveal specific training needs — knowing an archery shot is closed, self-paced and fine tells a coach to prioritise consistency of technique and mental routine rather than reaction speed or physical power; classifying a rugby tackle as open, externally paced and gross directs training towards reactive drills and contact conditioning rather than technical precision; using continuums prevents coaches from applying the wrong training prescription, e.g. drilling a rugby player in closed-skill repetition when open-skill adaptability is what match performance demands; continuums allow comparison of a performer's current skill level to the demands of the full game situation. Arguments against or limitations: classifying skills is time-consuming and most coaches work intuitively from experience; the four continuums may oversimplify — many skills shift along continuums depending on context (a tennis serve is closed when initiating but the rally is open); beginners may benefit more from straightforward 'easy/hard' progression than from theoretical classification. Justified conclusion: the four continuums are most useful when planning training progression, especially when designing drills that match real competition demands.

Secure: Two or three points on each side, mostly applied to both sports, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but thin or one-sport only.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application.

before.exam_tip_html: On 9-mark evaluate questions about goal setting, a common error is arguing only one side — for example, only criticising outcome goals without acknowledging any merit. To reach the highest band, you must consider both sides and apply your points to a sporting context. Structure each point as: state the idea → develop it → apply to a sporting example (e.g. “outcome goals can demotivate beginners because winning is unrealistic — a new tennis player facing a county-standard opponent may score zero games and feel they have completely failed, reducing their desire to continue”). On 3-mark describe or 4-mark explain questions asking you to describe a SMART target, always include the letter A stands for ‘accepted’ — not ‘achievable’ — as this is the most frequently penalised mistake.

before.content_html:
Why Feedback Matters in Sport

Every time a gymnast sticks a landing, a coach calls a correction, or a tennis player hears the crowd react to a shot, information is flowing. That information — feedback — is at the heart of how athletes learn, refine skills and progress. Without it, performers would repeat errors indefinitely. With the right type of feedback, delivered at the right moment, improvement accelerates.

The specification organises feedback into three overlapping categories: its emotional tone (positive or negative), its source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). A single piece of feedback can belong to more than one category simultaneously — for instance, a coach saying “that was an excellent drive, but your follow-through was cut short” is extrinsic, partly positive, partly negative, and contains knowledge of performance.

Positive and Negative Feedback

Positive feedback confirms that an action was performed correctly. It reinforces the movement pattern in the performer’s memory, making it more likely to be repeated. A coach saying “great shoulder rotation on that serve” or a crowd applauding a clean strike are both positive feedback. For beginners especially, positive feedback is powerful — it builds confidence and keeps motivation high at a stage when errors are frequent and self-belief is fragile.

Negative feedback highlights what went wrong and, ideally, what should be done differently. The term “negative” does not mean unkind or demoralising — it simply means the feedback signals a mismatch between what was intended and what was produced. A rugby coach who tells a player “your tackling angle is too narrow, step out wider next time” is giving negative feedback that is precise and constructive. Elite performers often seek and welcome negative feedback because they are confident enough to use it as a tool rather than a threat.

Key Fact

Positive feedback is especially important for beginners because it builds confidence and reinforces correct movements. Negative feedback becomes more valuable for elite performers, who need precise detail on how to refine already high-level technique.

Intrinsic and Extrinsic Feedback

Intrinsic feedback (also called internal feedback) comes from the performer’s own body. It travels through sensory channels: proprioception (the sense of where your limbs are in space), vision, touch and hearing. A gymnast knows her balance beam routine felt fluent because her proprioceptive system reports smooth weight transfer and correctly timed muscle contractions. A cricketer senses from the impact vibration through the bat handle whether the ball was struck from the middle of the bat. Intrinsic feedback is instantaneous and continuous — it arrives during and immediately after every movement.

For intrinsic feedback to be useful, the performer must have the experience and body awareness to interpret the sensations correctly. Beginners often struggle to do this — they may feel that a movement went well when it did not, because they lack the kinaesthetic reference point of what “correct” feels like. Elite athletes, by contrast, are highly attuned to intrinsic feedback: Mo Farah described being able to sense the precise moment his running economy started to drop in the final 200 m of a 5,000 m race.

Extrinsic feedback (external feedback) originates outside the performer. Sources include coaches and teachers, peers, video analysis, heart rate monitors, scoreboards and the crowd. Because it comes from outside, extrinsic feedback can fill the gaps that intrinsic feedback misses — for example, a sprinter cannot feel the exact angle of her block start, but her coach can see it on a camera and give precise corrections.

A common error is assuming that because intrinsic feedback is immediate, it must be accurate. Beginners lack the kinaesthetic memory to judge “correct” feeling — a novice swimmer may feel that her arm entry is clean when it is actually crossed over the midline. This is precisely why extrinsic feedback from a coach or video is so critical in early learning: it provides a reliable external reference point until the performer builds a more accurate internal model.

Knowledge of Results and Knowledge of Performance

Knowledge of results (KR) tells the performer what the outcome was: the shot went wide, the javelin landed at 42 metres, the race was completed in 13.8 seconds. It is always extrinsic because the result is separate from the movement itself. KR is easy to understand and motivating — seeing a time improve from 14.2 s to 13.8 s gives a clear signal that training is working — but it tells the performer nothing about why the result was what it was, or how to change it.

Knowledge of performance (KP) focuses on the quality of the movement: the hips rotated too early, the release angle was too flat, the elbow position was correct. KP is richer than KR and more directly actionable because it tells the performer what to change. A coach watching a discus thrower and saying “your pivot foot twisted before your non-throwing arm swept across — you lost rotation” is giving knowledge of performance. Elite performers typically benefit more from KP because their outcomes are already competitive and fine technical detail is what separates them from rivals.

Key Fact

Knowledge of results (KR) = the outcome (time, score, distance). Knowledge of performance (KP) = the quality of the technique. KR motivates; KP teaches. Elite performers need both, but KP is the more powerful learning tool.

Choosing the Right Feedback for the Performer

The effectiveness of feedback depends on the performer’s stage of learning. Beginners benefit most from positive feedback (to build confidence), extrinsic feedback (because intrinsic awareness is unreliable), and knowledge of results (which is simple to understand). Overloading a beginner with detailed KP can cause confusion and undermine motivation.

Elite performers, on the other hand, respond best to specific negative and positive feedback on technique (KP), as well as their own well-developed intrinsic feedback. They also benefit from extrinsic sources such as video analysis and data from performance monitoring equipment. The key principle is that feedback should always be actionable — vague comments such as “try harder” or “that was good” without further detail have little learning value regardless of the performer’s level.

In the basic information processing model you studied in the previous lesson, feedback is the final stage that loops back into the input. Intrinsic feedback feeds into the system through the sensory display (sight, touch, proprioception). Extrinsic feedback arrives as a new input — the coach’s voice or the video replay enters the input stage alongside environmental information from the display. Both types then influence decision making in the next attempt, helping the performer select a more appropriate motor response from long-term memory. This loop is why consistent, timely feedback speeds up skill acquisition.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Arousal is the level of physical and mental activation in a performer. The inverted-U theory shows that performance is best at an optimal arousal level — too little causes under-performance through lethargy; too much causes over-performance through anxiety and loss of fine motor control.
  • Optimal arousal varies by skill type: gross skills (tackling, sprinting, throwing) require higher arousal; fine skills (archery, snooker, a penalty kick) require lower arousal to preserve motor precision.
  • Three stress management techniques lower over-arousal: deep breathing (slows heart rate via the parasympathetic system), mental rehearsal/visualisation (simulates successful performance), and positive self-talk (replaces negative thoughts with affirming cues).

before.content_html:
What Are Engagement Patterns?

Engagement patterns describe who participates in physical activity, how often, and in which activities. They vary significantly across different social groups — not because of differences in ability, but because of the social, cultural, economic and practical factors that shape people’s lives. Understanding why participation differs between groups is central to this topic, because the goal of sport policy and education is to remove barriers and make physical activity genuinely accessible to all.

The specification identifies five social groups whose engagement patterns merit specific study: gender, race and religion (including culture), age, family and friends (peers), and people with a disability. For each group, a range of factors can either promote or discourage participation. These factors are not mutually exclusive — a person’s engagement is typically shaped by a combination of several simultaneously.

Gender and Engagement Patterns

Despite significant progress in recent decades, engagement patterns in the UK still differ between men and women. Women and girls historically face additional barriers that reduce their participation rates in many formal and competitive sports. Sexism and stereotyping play a documented role: cultural assumptions that sport is a male domain discourage participation, particularly at secondary school age when peer opinion carries heavy social weight. Media coverage is a powerful amplifier: women’s sport receives a fraction of broadcast time compared to men’s sport in most disciplines, which limits the visibility of female role models and reduces the perceived status of women’s sport.

Role models matter enormously to engagement. When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick in England’s opening game of the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euros, junior girls’ football club registrations spiked across England. Similarly, Dame Sarah Storey’s Paralympic cycling gold medals have been credited with increasing female disability sport participation. The absence of visible female role models in a sport creates a self-reinforcing cycle: girls don’t see women competing, so they don’t believe the sport is for them. Family commitments also fall disproportionately on women across all age groups, reducing available leisure time. Socio-economic factors intersect here too: lower-income households, where women are statistically over-represented, may have less disposable income to spend on sport memberships, equipment and travel.

Key Fact

Key factors limiting female engagement: sexism and stereotyping (cultural assumptions about suitability), limited media coverage (reduces role model visibility), family commitments (reduces available leisure time), and socio-economic factors (lower disposable income, fewer facilities in lower-income areas). Positive role models such as Beth Mead and Dame Sarah Storey have demonstrably increased participation.

Race, Religion and Culture

Engagement patterns can differ significantly between ethnic and religious groups. Race-based discrimination in sport — from unconscious bias in recruitment to overt racist behaviour from crowds — creates hostile environments that deter participation. In football, cricket and athletics, governing bodies have run high-profile campaigns to address racism, acknowledging that even elite sport is not free from this barrier.

Religion and culture add further dimensions. Religious festivals, prayer times and dietary requirements can create scheduling conflicts with training and competition. A Muslim athlete observing Ramadan fasts may find the energy demands of high-intensity training during that period challenging, requiring coaches and clubs to show flexibility. Cultural norms within some communities restrict female participation in mixed-sex sport or sport where clothing requirements conflict with modesty expectations. Familiarity also matters: if a sport has no visible presence within a particular cultural community, members of that community may not encounter it, learn its rules or perceive it as accessible. Education and community outreach can address this, but change is slow.

Age

Participation patterns change across the life course. Young people tend to participate at higher rates when physical education is compulsory, activity is part of the school day and peer social groups are built around sport. After leaving school, participation often drops sharply — a phenomenon described in research as the “dropout cliff” — as competing demands of higher education, work and family life reduce available leisure time and physical activity becomes optional rather than compulsory.

Older adults face different barriers: declining physical capacity, increased risk of injury, fewer accessible facilities, and reduced social networks following retirement or bereavement. However, accessible and appropriate activities — such as walking football, seated yoga, aqua aerobics and bowls — can sustain engagement among older populations. Attitudes towards ageing also matter: negative stereotypes around older people and sport discourage participation and undermine the confidence of individuals who might otherwise be active. The role of attitudes — both the individual’s own and those of those around them — is a consistent theme across all groups.

Family is one of the strongest predictors of physical activity in children. Children whose parents participate in sport are significantly more likely to be active themselves — parents model behaviour, provide transport, pay fees, and signal through their own choices that sport is worthwhile. Conversely, family commitments can be the biggest barrier to adult female participation in particular, as childcare and caring responsibilities disproportionately reduce available leisure time for women.

Peers carry enormous influence in adolescence: young people are more likely to participate if their friendship group is active, and more likely to drop out if sport is not part of their social identity. Socio-economic factors cut across all groups: socio-economic factors such as disposable income determine whether a family can afford club memberships, specialist equipment, coaching fees and travel. Free or low-cost community sport programmes are therefore critical to equitable access, particularly for young people in lower-income households.

Disability

People with physical or intellectual disabilities historically face some of the most significant barriers to participation in sport. These fall into physical and attitudinal categories. Physical barriers include inaccessible facilities (steps rather than ramps, no accessible changing rooms, pools without hoist equipment), lack of adapted equipment, and absence of disability-specific sessions or coaching. Attitudinal barriers are often harder to address: negative stereotypes assume that people with disabilities are not interested in or capable of sport at competitive level, despite extensive evidence to the contrary. Dame Sarah Storey’s 17 Paralympic gold medals, Jonnie Peacock’s 100 m sprint title at London 2012 and the growth of wheelchair basketball as a spectator sport all challenge these assumptions.

Adaptability and inclusiveness of facilities and activities are therefore key factors. Where clubs, leisure centres and governing bodies have invested in adaptive provision — deaf-friendly coaching, wheelchair-accessible courts, sitting volleyball, boccia, goalball — participation among disabled groups has increased. The relationship between disability and engagement underlines the broader principle: removing practical barriers and challenging negative attitudes are the twin levers for improving engagement patterns across all under-represented groups.

Key Fact

Barriers for disabled people: physical (inaccessible facilities, no adapted equipment, no disability sessions) and attitudinal (stereotyping, negative assumptions about capability and interest). Adaptability and inclusiveness of provision are the key solutions. Role models like Dame Sarah Storey and Jonnie Peacock challenge stereotypes and raise visibility.

Several factors appear as barriers across multiple groups, not just one. Role models: absence of visible, relatable role models reduces aspirational engagement for any under-represented group. Media coverage: low media coverage limits the perceived legitimacy and interest of a group’s participation. Accessibility: physical access to facilities matters across gender, age, disability and socio-economic status. Attitudes: both the individual’s own attitudes and the attitudes of coaches, clubs and institutions affect whether individuals feel welcome. Education: schools and community programmes that introduce diverse young people to a wide range of activities early build habits of participation that often persist into adulthood. Recognising these cross-cutting factors helps answer exam questions that ask you to explain multiple barriers or evaluate strategies to increase engagement.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about technology in sport, a common error is describing what technology does without explaining the impact. The mark scheme rewards analysis: state the technology, describe its effect, explain who benefits or loses out, and give a sporting example. Avoid vague statements such as “technology is good for sport” — be specific: “GPS tracking allows coaches to monitor a player’s sprint distance in training, enabling workload to be adjusted to reduce injury risk.” For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, always consider technology’s impact on multiple groups (performers, officials, audiences, sponsors) and ensure your argument addresses both benefits and drawbacks. One-sided answers are capped at the Developing band.

lessons.title: Performance Enhancing Drugs and Blood Doping

before.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about a specific PED category, give three distinct pieces of information: what the substance does, which type of performer might use it and why, and one side effect. Avoid the common error of repeating the same point in different words — for example, “it increases muscle mass” and “it helps muscles grow” are the same point and will only earn 1 mark. For a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question on whether PED use can ever be justified, you must present genuine arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion. A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the arguments athletes make for using them will be capped at the Developing band. Use the ‘For X… However Y…’ structure with a specific sporting type anchored to each side.

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a powerlifter who wants to increase muscle mass rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anabolic agents (1) or anabolic steroids (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood doping' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blood doping involves removing and re-infusing blood to increase red blood cell count; 1 mark for linking this to an improvement in oxygen-carrying capacity or endurance performance. Example full-mark answer: 'Blood doping is a prohibited method in which an athlete removes a quantity of their own blood weeks before competition, stores it, and re-infuses it just before competing in order to artificially increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the effects and side effects of using EPO as a performance-enhancing substance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that EPO increases red blood cell production; 1 mark for explaining that this increases oxygen-carrying capacity and benefits endurance performance; 1 mark for a valid side effect (blood thickening/increased viscosity; risk of heart attack or stroke; risk of blood clot/embolism). Example full-mark answer: 'EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells in the body (1). More red blood cells increase the blood’s ability to carry oxygen to working muscles, improving aerobic endurance performance (1). A dangerous side effect is that EPO thickens the blood, increasing viscosity, which can lead to blood clots, heart attack or stroke (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a performer might choose to use anabolic agents, and two reasons why this decision could have serious negative consequences for them.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons for + 2 consequences): must cover both sides for full marks.
Reasons for using (up to 2 marks): increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); increased chance of competition success leading to financial reward and recognition (1).
Negative consequences (up to 2 marks): risk of liver damage and cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption, including in secondary sexual characteristics (1); risk of ban, fine and permanent reputational damage if detected (1); permanent growth plate damage in adolescent users (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level distance runner has been told by a teammate that EPO is undetectable and that many top competitors use it anyway. Evaluate the arguments for and against the runner using EPO, and reach a conclusion about whether such arguments can be justified.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Challenges the ‘level playing field’ reasoning with counter-arguments. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (red blood cells, oxygen-carrying capacity, viscosity). Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application throughout.
Secure: Covers arguments for and against EPO use; mostly accurate physiological understanding; mostly applied to an endurance sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.
Emerging: Basic statements that EPO is wrong or helpful without physiological explanation; no balanced argument; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for using EPO: increased red blood cells improve oxygen delivery to muscles, directly improving endurance performance; may be perceived as levelling the field if others are doping; potential for greater competition success, fame and financial reward; if truly undetectable, perceived risk of sanction is low.
Arguments against using EPO: blood thickening significantly raises risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — particularly dangerous during sleep when heart rate is low; the ‘level playing field’ argument is flawed because many competitors do not dope; wealthier competitors access safer protocols creating new inequalities; if detected, consequences include lengthy ban, loss of results, fines and career-ending reputational damage; the use violates the contract to compete and the ethical foundations of sport; the sport of distance running suffers credibility damage from doping scandals, reducing sponsorship and audience engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two side effects of blood doping for a performer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct side effects, or 1 mark for identifying the mechanism and 1 mark for explaining the consequence. Acceptable side effects: thickening of blood/increased viscosity (1); risk of heart attack (1); risk of stroke/embolism/blockage of a blood vessel (1); potential infection from contaminated equipment (1); risk from the transfusion process itself (1). Example 3-mark answer: 'Blood doping causes the blood to thicken as red blood cell count increases (1). This increased viscosity slows blood flow and raises the risk of a heart attack (1). There is also a risk of embolism — a blockage of a blood vessel — which can be fatal (1).'

The benefit gained from playing in a familiar venue with crowd support
A rule giving the home team extra time in finals
An advantage gained by practising at home the night before a match

knowledge_checks.q: Which anti-hooliganism strategy requires known offenders to surrender their passport during international fixtures?
_____ of fans involves placing rival supporters in separate sections of the stadium to prevent direct confrontation.
Scheduling games for _____ kick-off times reduces the opportunity for pre-match drinking.
Match each cause of hooliganism to the most appropriate anti-hooliganism strategy:
left: Lack of awareness and cultural norms

before.content_html:
Spectators: A Force for Good and Ill

Sporting events exist, in large part, because of spectators. The roar of a packed stadium, the wave of noise that greets a home goal, the nervous hush before a penalty — all of these are products of crowd presence. Yet that same crowd can become a source of danger, intimidation and reputational damage if behaviour breaks down. Understanding the dual nature of spectator influence is essential for any student of sport.

Home advantage is one of the clearest positive effects of a crowd. Research in English football consistently shows that home teams win more often than away teams. The reasons are several: players feed off crowd energy, officials may be subconsciously influenced by the home crowd’s reactions, and away teams carry the psychological burden of hostile noise. In athletics, a partisan stadium crowd can lift a 400-metre runner through the final bend in a way that an empty track simply cannot replicate.

Key Fact

Spectators generate atmosphere and can provide a significant home advantage. However, they can also create excessive pressure, trigger crowd trouble and pose safety risks — all of which can harm both performance and the wider reputation of a sport.

Positive Effects of Spectators

Beyond home advantage, spectators contribute to the financial sustainability of sport. Gate receipts, broadcast rights and sponsorship are all driven by audience size. A full stadium signals a healthy, commercially attractive sport. For young performers in particular, crowd support can be a powerful intrinsic motivator: seeing others invest emotion in your performance reinforces a sense of belonging and purpose. High-profile events broadcast to millions can also inspire young people to take up a sport, widening engagement patterns in the population.

Negative Effects of Spectators

The negative effects of spectators are equally significant. Crowd noise and hostile atmosphere can increase a performer’s arousal beyond the optimal level, tipping them into over-arousal and a deterioration in performance — a concept explored in the inverted-U theory covered in Lesson 10. An away goalkeeper pelted with abuse before a penalty shoot-out is being subjected to deliberate psychological disruption. Even without overt hostility, the weight of a large crowd’s expectations can cause anxiety and choking in performers who struggle to manage their mental state.

More seriously, spectators who move beyond verbal hostility into physical confrontation create a public order crisis. Hooliganism is the collective term for this behaviour, and it has been a significant problem in English football since at least the 1960s. Hooliganism causes direct harm to individuals, destroys the spectator experience for law-abiding fans, generates enormous policing costs and has led to English clubs being banned from European competition (following the Heysel stadium disaster of 1985). The knock-on effect for grassroots participation is real: younger players and families are deterred from attending or playing if they associate the sport with violence.

Hooliganism rarely has a single cause. The spec identifies a range of overlapping factors:

  • Rivalries: historic or local rivalries (city derbies, regional contests) intensify emotional investment to the point where hostility feels justified.
  • Hype: media build-up can manufacture a sense of occasion that encourages aggressive group identity.
  • Alcohol and drugs: disinhibit behaviour and reduce the individual’s risk calculation.
  • Frustration: poor refereeing decisions or a losing scoreline can trigger reactive aggression in crowd members already emotionally primed.
  • Gang culture: for some groups, attending a match is a vehicle for pre-organised violence unconnected to the sport itself.
  • Display of masculinity: sociological research suggests that for certain subcultures, hooliganism functions as a performance of toughness, with crowd disorder reinforcing group identity and status.

Understanding these causes is important because the effectiveness of control strategies depends on which causes they address. Alcohol restrictions tackle disinhibition; education campaigns tackle culture; banning orders target repeat offenders regardless of cause.

Strategies to Combat Hooliganism

Authorities have introduced numerous strategies to reduce hooliganism, and you need to be able to evaluate how effective each one is:

All-seater stadia: following the Taylor Report (1990), English top-flight grounds converted to all-seater venues. Seating reduces the anonymity of standing crowds, makes identification of offenders easier and creates a calmer physical environment. Critics argue that it has reduced atmosphere without fully eliminating disorder, and that it has priced out working-class supporters.

Segregation of fans: away supporters are allocated separate sections with barriers between them. This physically prevents the kind of confrontation between rival groups that sparks disorder. It is highly effective at the ground but displaces the problem to the streets before and after matches.

Alcohol restrictions: alcohol cannot be consumed in view of the pitch at English Football League grounds. Some high-risk matches have total alcohol bans or enforce dry trains. Alcohol is strongly correlated with disinhibited behaviour, so restrictions have a measurable effect, though determined individuals can pre-load before arriving at the stadium.

Early kick-offs: scheduling games for 12:00 or 12:30 reduces the time available for pre-match drinking, particularly for away supporters who travel by train. This is a cost-effective measure that requires no additional infrastructure.

Improved security and CCTV: increased steward numbers, police presence and extensive CCTV coverage deter disorder through visibility and the certainty of identification. CCTV also allows retrospective prosecution, contributing to successful banning order applications.

Banning orders are now the primary tool for managing persistent offenders. Courts issue them following convictions or civil applications by police. Individuals subject to a banning order must report to a police station during international matches, preventing travel abroad. Since their introduction, banning orders have reduced the number of known England hooligan offenders travelling to tournaments significantly.

Travel restrictions complement banning orders by limiting access to fixtures for away supporters in high-risk categories. Ticket-only travel schemes on official coaches reduce the number of unaccounted individuals in transit.

Education and campaigns: initiatives such as “Kick It Out” and football club community programmes aim at cultural change over the longer term. High-profile endorsements by respected athletes and ex-players carry credibility with young fans. This is the most sustainable strategy but the slowest to produce results and the hardest to evaluate with data.

Arrest statistics at English football matches have fallen substantially since the early 1990s. Compared to the period when standing terraces and minimal segregation were the norm, English football today is dramatically safer for spectators. The combination of structural changes (all-seater stadia, segregation) with legal tools (banning orders) and cultural programmes has produced genuine progress.

However, there are costs and limitations. All-seater stadia require significant capital investment — a barrier for lower-league clubs. Security staffing is expensive and is often passed on to supporters through ticket prices. Banning orders require police resource to monitor and enforce. Critics also point out that online abuse and discriminatory chanting remain difficult to prosecute and represent a continuation of spectator harm in a different form. The safest honest assessment is that physical violence has been substantially reduced but the underlying attitudes that cause it have not been fully addressed.

Key Fact

The seven main anti-hooliganism strategies are: all-seater stadia, segregation, alcohol restrictions, early kick-offs, improved security/CCTV, banning orders and education/campaigns. In an extended-response question, evaluate each on effectiveness, cost and whether it addresses the root cause or just the symptom.

What Do We Mean by Health and Wellbeing?

Health is not simply the absence of illness. The World Health Organisation defines it as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — a definition that has shaped how GCSE PE approaches this topic. A person can be physically fit (able to run five kilometres without stopping) yet struggle with anxiety, loneliness or low self-worth. True wellbeing is multi-dimensional, and physical activity affects all three dimensions simultaneously, which is what makes it one of the most powerful public health tools available.

This lesson examines each dimension in turn: physical health, mental health and social health. Each is an equal component of overall wellbeing, and a physically active lifestyle improves all three.

Key Fact

Participation in physical activity improves health across three dimensions: physical (heart function, body systems, disease prevention), mental (stress reduction, hormone release, emotional control) and social (friendships, teamwork, community). These three dimensions are interconnected — improving one often improves the others.

Physical Health and Wellbeing

The physical benefits of regular exercise are the most visible and the most extensively researched. Regular aerobic activity — whether swimming, cycling, running or team sport — strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume (the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat) and reduces resting heart rate. The result is a more efficient cardiovascular system that can deliver oxygen to working muscles more effectively during exercise and recover more quickly afterwards. Athletes who train consistently over years develop bradycardia, a resting heart rate well below the population average of 70 beats per minute.

Beyond the heart, regular exercise improves the efficiency of the respiratory system, the musculoskeletal system and the immune system. The lungs become more efficient at gas exchange; muscles grow stronger and more fatigue-resistant; bones maintain their density and reduce the risk of osteoporosis in later life. These systemic benefits mean a physically active person is better equipped to perform everyday tasks (carrying shopping, climbing stairs, walking to work) and is less likely to suffer from a range of chronic diseases including type 2 diabetes, certain cancers and hypertension.

One of the clearest population-level physical benefits of exercise is its role in weight management. Regular activity burns calories, maintains muscle mass and supports a healthy body composition. This helps avoid obesity, which is itself a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes and reduced mobility. The physical and the social are already beginning to connect: an individual who maintains a healthy weight through sport is also likely to have the physical capacity to engage with others in activity, creating a positive feedback loop.

Mental Health and Wellbeing

The mental health benefits of exercise are now backed by a substantial body of clinical research and are increasingly recognised by healthcare systems as a legitimate treatment for mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression. The mechanisms are both biochemical and psychological.

At the biochemical level, moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of happiness and calm. It also promotes the release of endorphins — natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce the so-called “runner’s high” familiar to distance athletes. The neurological effect of these hormones is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. For many individuals, a vigorous training session or team sport match functions as a reliable, accessible and side-effect-free stress management tool.

Beyond hormones, physical activity provides psychological benefits through mastery and control. Setting a personal best, learning a new skill or winning a team competition builds self-efficacy — the belief in one’s own capacity to succeed. This is particularly powerful for young people, for whom sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in other areas of life. The ability to control emotions during competition (remain calm under pressure, manage frustration after a mistake) transfers directly to emotional regulation in daily life. These mental benefits are why sport is used therapeutically in programmes for young people experiencing mental health difficulties.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. In short bursts this is useful; chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a “legitimate outlet” for the physiological state stress creates. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events. This is why mental health professionals increasingly recommend structured physical activity as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Health and Wellbeing

Humans are social animals. The sense of belonging to a group, having friends and being valued by a community are fundamental psychological needs. Sport and physical activity are remarkably powerful vehicles for meeting these needs, which is why social health is a genuine and distinct category in the wellbeing framework.

Team sports in particular demand cooperation and teamwork. Playing in a netball team, a cricket XI or a rowing eight requires communication, trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These are not merely sporting skills: they are life skills transferable to workplaces, families and communities. Young people who participate in team sport regularly develop stronger interpersonal skills and a better understanding of how to negotiate conflict constructively.

Participation also creates opportunities to socialise and make friends. For individuals who are isolated — whether through geography, disability, mental health difficulties or life transitions such as moving to a new school — joining a sports club can be the single most effective intervention for reducing loneliness. Sport provides a structured social context with shared purpose, which lowers the social anxiety of unstructured socialisation. Community sport clubs also play a direct role in meeting basic social needs by connecting individuals to wider networks of mutual support.

Students sometimes assume that wellbeing benefits require competitive, high-intensity sport. This is not what the spec says, and it is not supported by the evidence. The physical, mental and social benefits of physical activity are available across a spectrum from gentle recreational walking through to elite competition. What matters is regular participation, not intensity or competitive context.

Indeed, for some individuals — particularly those recovering from mental health difficulties, or older adults entering exercise for the first time — low-intensity, non-competitive activity (yoga, social swimming, walking groups) may produce greater wellbeing gains precisely because it is accessible, enjoyable and sustainable. The spec asks you to recognise that physical activity broadly encompasses all forms of movement, not just sport.

Key Fact

For extended-response questions on wellbeing, make sure you address all three dimensions with a sporting example for each. A common error is to write only about physical benefits. Mental (serotonin, stress, emotional control) and social (teamwork, cooperation, socialisation) benefits carry equal mark-scheme weight.

Energy: The Fuel for Sport and Life

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy is measured in kilocalories (Kcal) and comes entirely from the food we eat. The average adult male requires approximately 2,500 Kcal per day, while the average adult female requires around 2,000 Kcal per day. However, these are only averages — how much energy any individual actually needs depends on four key factors: age, gender, height, and energy expenditure (how much exercise they do). A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same height and gender.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, height, and energy expenditure. Average values are 2,500 Kcal/day for males and 2,000 Kcal/day for females — but athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more.

The Balanced Diet: Proportions and Purposes

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. Unused energy, particularly from saturated fats, is stored as body fat, which can contribute to obesity over time. The specification requires you to know the approximate percentage breakdown of a balanced diet: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein. These proportions reflect the primary roles each macronutrient plays in the body.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners such as Dina Asher-Smith prepare for competition partly by ensuring glycogen stores are fully loaded through carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects organs, and is a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins.

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty, for example, follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the adaptations (such as hypertrophy) that training is designed to produce.

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function to bone health; minerals such as calcium and iron are vital for bone density and oxygen transport in the blood respectively. The specification does not require you to name specific vitamins or minerals, but you should know that their role is to maintain the efficient working of body systems and general health. A diet lacking in variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its Kcal total looks adequate on paper.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is not just a drink — it is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance (hydration) is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In severe cases, heart rhythm may become irregular. Meanwhile, the body’s ability to shed heat through the blood vessels near the skin is compromised, causing core body temperature to rise — increasing the risk of overheating and heat stroke.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. For a sprint cyclist like Geraint Thomas, any cramping or slowing of reaction time in the final kilometre of a race could be decisive.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The spec focuses on balance — maintaining appropriate water levels, not overloading with fluids. The assessment reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: thicker blood → higher heart rate → slower delivery of oxygen → muscle fatigue/cramp → slower reactions → poorer decisions. Practise writing that chain in order without notes, anchored to a sporting example.
